title: GFP Chief Vijai Sardesai Alleges Nepal Citizens Added to Voter Rolls During SIR, Seeks Probe - Deccan Chronicle
description: GFP Chief Vijai Sardesai Alleges Nepal Citizens Added to Voter Rolls During SIR, Seeks Probe  Deccan Chronicle
publisher.title: Deccan Chronicle
full_article:
Panaji: Goa Forward Party (GFP) chief and MLA Vijai Sardesai on Saturday alleged that Nepalese nationals were added as voters in the state during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and demanded an "impartial and time-bound" investigation into the alleged "irregularities".Addressing a press conference here, Sardesai said some "invisible" voters were added to the electoral list, while eligible people were finding their names missing from the rolls.

"Nepalese nationals have been added as voters in Goa during the SIR exercise. How can any foreign national be a part of India's electoral roll?" he asked.

"We will now have to conduct street plays to create awareness among the voters, asking them to check whether their names are there in the rolls or not," Sardesai said, giving examples of how several voters from his constituency found their names getting deleted from the list without their knowledge.

The Fatorda MLA also lodged a complaint with the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), alleging that more than 50 voters were illegally shifted from the Curtorim assembly constituency to Fatorda even as their addresses remained the same.

Sardesai submitted the complaint via email on Friday, seeking an impartial and time-bound investigation into the alleged irregularities in electoral rolls.

The former deputy chief minister claimed in his complaint that names of several voters, who were in the Curtorim constituency during the 2012 and 2017 assembly elections, figured in the Fatorda electoral rolls in 2022 and 2026.

He alleged that the purported transfers raised concerns over the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls and compliance with statutory provisions governing voter registration and constituency boundaries.

Describing the alleged irregularities as "merely the tip of the iceberg", Sardesai sought the CEO's urgent intervention to investigate a "deliberate attempt to manipulate electoral records".

The complaint referred to the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and relevant Election Commission of India guidelines, stressing that electoral registration must conform to legally notified constituency boundaries and the requirement of ordinary residence.

Sardesai also sought the deletion of voter entries found to have been illegally shifted, disciplinary action and criminal prosecution against those found responsible, and a state-wide audit to ascertain whether similar irregularities had occurred in other constituencies.

The legislator submitted annexures containing voter details from the Curtorim electoral rolls for 2012 and 2017 and the Fatorda rolls for 2021 and 2026 in support of his allegations.

Sardesai's allegations come amid INDIA bloc and Cockroach Janta Party's protests over demand for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities and mass voter deletions during the SIR of electoral rolls.

title: Nepal’s Deadly Flood Puts Its Always On Health System to the Test - Bioengineer.org
description: Nepal’s Deadly Flood Puts Its Always On Health System to the Test  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
On 26 August 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche on Nepal’s northern border with China sent a violent flash flood surging down the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor, and the numbers that followed have forced public health experts to rethink what a flood actually is. By 25 September, Nepal’s disaster authority had confirmed 1,453 deaths, recorded 5,285 people as missing, rescued 13,795 survivors, and logged 10,988 people needing medical treatment. Writing in PLOS Global Public Health, Krishna Kumar Aryal of the University of Bergen and colleagues argue that these figures demand a conceptual shift: a flood of this magnitude should be counted as a burden-of-disease event, not merely a rescue operation, and the health system’s performance should be judged across preparedness, response, and long-term resilience rather than by the drama of the emergency alone.

The arithmetic behind that claim is stark. The confirmed deaths alone already outrank seven of the twenty-one causes of death that Nepal routinely tracks. If the missing are eventually confirmed dead, this single event would fall within the top ten leading causes of death in a typical year. To put that in perspective, if everyone missing is confirmed dead, the flood will have killed nearly as many people in Nepal as diabetes does annually, a chronic condition that claimed 7,976 lives in 2023. Burden-of-disease accounting, built on the Global Burden of Disease framework, normally assigns deaths to categories like cardiovascular disease, respiratory infections, or diabetes. Disasters are usually treated as one-off shocks outside that ledger. Aryal and colleagues contend that this accounting habit obscures the true health toll of climate-driven catastrophes and lets health systems escape the scrutiny that a comparable epidemic would trigger.

The health system itself was a casualty of the flood. Four health facilities and two warehouses were destroyed, three more facilities damaged, and 19 health workers went missing. Thirty-five motorable bridges and 45 suspension bridges were washed away, severing access to secondary-level care at Nuwakot and Dhading district hospitals in already hard-to-reach mountain terrain. Within 24 hours, disease surveillance recorded cases of acute gastroenteritis, influenza-like illness, and fever-with-rash at displacement sites, while a third of the water samples tested were contaminated. These are the classic early signatures of outbreak risk when water, sanitation, and referral systems fail together. With thousands of people still living in temporary shelters, the authors warn that the risk of further communicable disease outbreaks remains high, and that the surveillance capacity that caught the first signals must be sustained, not switched off once the headlines fade.

Nepal has faced this test before, four times at major scale in nine years: the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, the 2017 Terai floods, the 2023 Jajarkot earthquake, and the 2024 floods and landslides. Each time, facilities were damaged or cut off, referral routes were lost, and immunisation and maternal services were disrupted. And each time, the country rebuilt to the same standard rather than a higher one. The 2026 flood is the fifth major rapid-onset disaster to strike along the same fault lines in barely a decade, and the authors argue that this repetition is itself the finding: the pattern reveals a system that responds heroically but does not convert experience into standing capability.

That distinction between nominal functioning and genuine resilience is central to the article’s technical argument. Resilience has often been measured simply by whether services continued during a shock. But a 2023 reconceptualization by health policy researcher Sophie Witter and colleagues, published in The Lancet Global Health, reframes the question around equity: not whether the system kept functioning, but who absorbed the strain of it doing so. In this flood, the answer is already visible in the demographic breakdown of who is left to cope. According to United Nations flash appeal figures, 19,284 households and 84,270 people were affected, including 43,085 women, 32,021 children and adolescents, of whom 7,048 were under five, 1,854 people with disabilities, and 8,603 elderly people. Resilience, the authors argue, will be judged less by the emergency response than by what follows: how quickly facilities are rebuilt and routine maternal, newborn, and non-communicable disease care is restored for these populations.

The conceptual benchmark the authors invoke comes from the fourth edition of Disease Control Priorities, or DCP4, a major global priority-setting initiative. DCP4 argues that health systems should be Always On, meaning that standing emergency capability should be built into routine care rather than assembled after the fact, through dual-use infrastructure that scales up during crises rather than switching on. Nepal has been building toward this since 2015. The country established Health Emergency Operation Centres, developed a hub-and-satellite referral system, adopted minimum service standards, expanded oxygen and laboratory capacity during COVID-19, and deployed Emergency Medical Deployment Teams alongside community surveillance and hospital disaster plans. A 2025 assessment of 25 Nepali hub hospitals found that most now hold standing disaster preparedness plans with provisions for surge capacity, coordinating emergency response and referrals across the federal system.

Yet the flood is a live audit of that investment, and so far the answers are discouraging. Did the destroyed health posts have any dual-use or surge design? Did referral protocols anticipate losing 80 bridges at once? The authors conclude that the answer to both questions looks like no. In a federal system, being Always On is as much a governance challenge as a technical one. Sustaining standing capabilities requires clear ownership, reliable financing, and coordinated preparedness across all tiers of government. But research mapping health system resilience at the local level in federal Nepal, published in BMC Health Services Research in 2025, found that legal responsibilities at the local tier still exceed the capacity and resources available to fulfil them. Accountability for rebuilding and maintaining surge readiness remains fragmented, while funds and support often reach the front line slowly. The flood therefore tests not only physical infrastructure but also the effectiveness of intergovernmental fiscal transfers, institutional coordination, and shared responsibility across Nepal’s three tiers of government.

The stakes extend well beyond the injured. After the 2015 earthquake, as the health system prioritised trauma care over routine services, admissions for maternal and other routine conditions at a Kathmandu tertiary hospital fell sharply and stayed low for months, a finding published in Scientific Reports in 2020 that shows a disaster’s harm reaches far beyond the injured. Mental health tells a similar story. Following the 2015 earthquake, psychosocial needs increased sharply, but the response was largely improvised because mental health support had not been adequately integrated into emergency preparedness plans, a gap documented in the WHO South-East Asia Journal of Public Health. The authors argue that a standing system should close both gaps by design. Health workers are among the affected too, with 19 missing in this flood, so safeguarding their wellbeing and swift return to work is itself part of keeping care running. Protecting routine care, they write, is what keeps this flood from adding a second, quieter toll to Nepal’s burden of disease.

Rebuilding to disaster-resilient standards helps, but at this scale it is not enough, because anything fixed in place can be swept away again. What must hold, the authors argue, is the referral network actually activated rather than assumed, with strategic facilities resourced and ready; emergency transport that reaches patients in time to prevent avoidable deaths; and humanitarian aid that reaches frontline health workers so they can return to work quickly. Nepal is now finalising its national health benefits package through a systematic priority-setting exercise toward universal health coverage by 2030, and the authors, several of whom support this work at Nepal’s Ministry of Health and Food Safety, see one concrete avenue: building continuity of basic services, including essential emergency and critical care, into the revised basic health services package as a standing requirement rather than an emergency add-on. Essential emergency and critical care, a concept defined through a global consensus of clinical experts published in BMJ Global Health in 2021, refers to the basic life-saving interventions, triage, oxygen, fluids, and monitoring, that every facility should deliver continuously.

Financing that standing capacity as routine health spending, rather than mobilising it as relief after each disaster, is the policy test this flood now sets. The authors call for funding essential services, including essential emergency and critical care, through recurrent budget lines and regular fiscal transfers to provincial and local governments, ensuring readiness is maintained between disasters rather than rebuilt after each shock. Nepal’s own disaster law already mandates such funds across all three tiers of government, yet local resources and financial flexibility remain limited. Global experience reinforces the point: analysis of the COVID-19 response, published in The Lancet in 2021, found that health security pursued in parallel to universal health coverage, rather than integrated with it, left systems fragmented and exposed, and that building preparedness into the routine systems and budgets that deliver everyday care is a more resilient course for low- and middle-income countries. The authors echo a view published in The Lancet while their paper was being finalised, by Karkey, Adhikari, and Basnyat, that health systems must be ready to absorb shocks of this magnitude while sustaining essential services. Nepal’s flood, they conclude, is the audit: counted properly, it becomes a burden-of-disease event that the health system must answer for, not just a rescue story it can be proud of.

title: Balen Shah picks India, not China, for first bilateral foreign trip as Nepal Prime Minister - The Indian Panorama
description: Balen Shah picks India, not China, for first bilateral foreign trip as Nepal Prime Minister  The Indian Panorama
publisher.title: The Indian Panorama
full_article:
Colombo (TIP): Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah (Balen Shah) is preparing to visit India in November, nearly eight months after taking office in March.

The three-day visit, expected in the third or fourth week of November, would be his first official bilateral trip abroad, although he travelled to the US in September for the United Nations General Assembly, where he spoke about a broken system’s threat to Nepal, Bangladesh, India and other South Asian nations.

From major infrastructure projects to border disputes and flood reconstruction, Balen Shah’s India visit is expected to have a packed agenda, reported The Kathmandu Post.

India has traditionally been the first foreign destination for Nepal’s prime ministers. However, Pushpa Kamal Dahal Prachanda chose China in 2008, Jhalanath Khanal visited Turkey in 2011 for a multilateral UN meet, and Sher Bahadur Deuba went to the UK in 2021 for the COP26. Oli, who had earlier chosen to visit India after assuming the top office, broke with the India-first tradition in December 2024 by choosing China for his first foreign visit after returning to power. Oli had claimed that India had not invited him for an official visit.

The timing of Balen Shah’s visit is significant, given Shah’s initial reluctance to engage with foreign diplomats, including those from India and China. It also comes after devastating floods in August, when India rushed relief supplies and rescue specialists to Nepal. Although preparations are underway, neither Kathmandu nor New Delhi has officially announced the dates of the visit.

Balen’s reported visit in November follows a high-profile trip to New Delhi by Rabi Lamichhane, president of Nepal’s ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), in June. Lamichhane received a ceremonial welcome at the BJP headquarters and met senior party leaders. The outreach drew attention because of Shah’s reserved approach towards diplomatic engagement. Lamichhane’s welcome was also intended to send a political message to the Nepali prime minister, veteran Nepal journalist Keshav Pradhan told India Today Digital in June.

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has taken the oath of office and secrecy at the party’s central office in Sanepa.

Thapa took the oath at a ceremony held at the party headquarters on Friday. Senior Vice-President Bishwa Prakash Sharma placed a garland of dubo grass around his neck during the ceremony.

title: Community Mental Health Program in Nepal Offers Hope for Migrant Families, Study Finds - Bioengineer.org
description: Community Mental Health Program in Nepal Offers Hope for Migrant Families, Study Finds  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
In the remote hills and plains of Nepal, where labor migration has become a defining feature of family life, a community-based mental health project is offering a rare window into the psychological toll of separation—and the potential of grassroots support to ease it. A new cross-sectional endline evaluation of the PARBARDHAN project, published in PLOS Global Public Health, documents the mental health and psychosocial wellbeing of people living in migration-affected communities in Salyan and Kailali districts, revealing both encouraging signs of reduced anxiety and depression and persistent, deeply rooted sources of distress.

The PARBARDHAN project was designed around a simple but ambitious premise: that mental health and psychosocial support can be strengthened not only through clinics and specialists, but through the communities themselves. By building local service capacity, fostering community participation, and embedding support mechanisms into everyday social life, the project sought to address the psychological consequences of labor migration for the workers who leave and the families who stay behind. The endline evaluation, conducted between February 3 and February 26, 2026, was intended to capture the state of psychosocial wellbeing after years of intervention activity, and to compare it descriptively with earlier baseline and midline assessment rounds.

The research team, led by Himal Gaire and colleagues, employed a mixed-methods design that combined quantitative screening with qualitative inquiry. The quantitative component enrolled 245 project beneficiaries aged between 16 and 80 years. Of these, 20 participants—8.2 percent of the sample—were migrant or returnee workers themselves, while the remaining 225, or 91.8 percent, were family or community respondents. The overwhelming majority of participants, 216 individuals or 88.2 percent, reported having a family member currently working abroad, underscoring how thoroughly migration has woven itself into the social fabric of these districts.

Psychological distress was measured using the General Health Questionnaire, a widely validated 12-item screening instrument known as the GHQ-12, which captures recent declines in general mental functioning, including symptoms of anxiety, insomnia, social dysfunction, and severe depression. Anxiety and depression were assessed separately using the Hopkins Symptom Checklist, or HSCL-25, a 25-item instrument that quantifies the frequency of anxiety and depressive symptoms over the preceding weeks. Beyond these clinical screening tools, the researchers also measured life satisfaction and subjective happiness, providing a broader picture of how participants evaluated their own wellbeing beyond symptom counts.

The headline quantitative findings present a nuanced picture. At endline, 34.7 percent of participants screened positive for psychological distress on the GHQ-12, while 8.2 percent screened positive for anxiety and 5.3 percent for depression on the HSCL-25. When the researchers compared these endline figures with the baseline and midline rounds, they found that screening positivity for anxiety and depression was lower at endline than at either of the two earlier assessment points. Probable psychological distress, however, was higher at endline than in previous rounds—a divergence that the authors interpret with caution, given the design constraints of the evaluation.

That caution is central to understanding what the study can and cannot tell us. Because each evaluation round used independent cross-sectional samples rather than following the same individuals over time, the observed differences cannot be interpreted as within-person changes, nor can they be attributed causally to the PARBARDHAN intervention. A lower rate of anxiety and depression at endline may reflect genuine improvement in the community’s mental health landscape, but it could also reflect differences in sample composition, seasonal factors, or the broader social and economic context at the time of data collection. Similarly, the higher rate of probable psychological distress may signal rising economic pressures rather than any failure of the intervention itself. The authors are explicit that these are descriptive comparisons, not causal claims.

The qualitative component of the evaluation, drawn from in-depth interviews and focus group discussions and analyzed using framework analysis, adds a rich contextual layer that the numbers alone cannot provide. Participants reported increased mental health awareness across their communities, a greater willingness to seek support when struggling, and perceived reductions in the stigma that has long surrounded mental illness in rural Nepal. Self-help groups, peer group counseling sessions, and community activities emerged as the mechanisms through which support was most visibly delivered, suggesting that the project’s community-based architecture succeeded in creating spaces where psychological distress could be acknowledged and addressed without shame.

Yet the qualitative findings also revealed a sobering counterpoint: substantial dissatisfaction with life persisted among many respondents. This dissatisfaction was intertwined with the structural realities that no amount of counseling can dissolve—economic insecurity that keeps families dependent on remittances, the prolonged separation of spouses and parents from their loved ones, and the uncertainty that shadows every migration decision. The authors emphasize that these structural factors continue to shape psychosocial wellbeing in ways that community-based support can mitigate but not eliminate. Mental health programming, in other words, operates within a larger social and economic environment that ultimately determines how much distress a community must carry.

The significance of the study extends beyond the two districts where data were collected. Nepal is one of the world’s most migration-dependent countries, with hundreds of thousands of workers leaving annually for destinations across the Gulf, Malaysia, and India. The families left behind—often headed by women, elderly members, or adolescents—face a distinctive constellation of psychosocial challenges: the emotional strain of separation, the burden of managing households alone, and the anxiety that accompanies news of workplace accidents or exploitation abroad. Community-based mental health and psychosocial support models like PARBARDHAN’s offer a scalable response precisely because they do not depend on scarce clinical specialists, instead mobilizing trained community members and peer networks to deliver basic support and referral pathways.

The evaluation’s findings indicate the perceived value of community-based mental health and psychosocial support among beneficiaries, while simultaneously highlighting the continuing economic insecurity, family separation, and other structural factors that affect psychosocial wellbeing in migration-affected communities. For policymakers and public health practitioners, the study suggests that investing in community-level mental health infrastructure can raise awareness, reduce stigma, and increase help-seeking behavior—outcomes that are themselves meaningful markers of progress even in the absence of causal certainty. But it also serves as a reminder that mental health interventions cannot substitute for broader structural change. As long as economic precarity drives mass labor migration and separates families for years at a time, the psychological burden on Nepal’s communities will remain substantial, and community-based support will remain a necessary but insufficient tool in the response.

Nepal's devastating floods should be a turning point for global climate action, with the international community helping the Himalayan nation recover, a top UN official told AFP on Saturday.

The country suffered one of the worst disasters in its history on August 26, when a mountain collapse near the China border triggered catastrophic floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

Scientists said climate change played a significant role in that disaster.

title: Nepal suffer shock defeat to Canada ahead of crucial Oman clash - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal suffer shock defeat to Canada ahead of crucial Oman clash  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal suffered a 24-run defeat to Canada in the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup League 2 on Saturday, missing the chance to strengthen their position in the race to finish sixth.

Canada posted 256 before bowling Nepal out for 232 in 46 overs at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Oman.

After winning the toss and opting to bat, Canada made a strong start through Yuvraj Samra and Aaron Johnson, who put on 72 runs for the opening wicket. Lalit Rajbanshi broke the partnership by bowling Johnson.

Samit Gohel scored 17 before Samra joined Harsh Thaker for an 88-run stand for the third wicket. Thaker contributed 34, while Samra went on to score 105 off 117 balls, hitting 11 fours and four sixes.

Samra was caught by Karan KC off Dipendra Singh Airee, having scored his maiden one-day international century. Canada captain Hamza Tariq added 34, but Nepal’s bowlers fought back in the latter stages, taking eight wickets for 65 runs.

Rajbanshi was Nepal’s leading bowler with four wickets for 39 runs in 10 overs. Captain Sandeep Lamichhane took three wickets, bringing his tally in the current League 2 cycle to 50. Airee claimed two wickets and Rohit Paudel one.

Chasing 257, Nepal struggled to build partnerships. Arjun Kumal top-scored with 87, recording his maiden ODI half-century, but lacked sufficient support from the other batters. Openers Aasif Sheikh and Ishan Pandey scored 20 and 21 respectively, while Paudel made 18 and Airee 27.

Gulshan Jha scored 21 before being dismissed, adding to Nepal’s pressure. Karan KC remained unbeaten on 17, but Nepal were eventually bowled out for 232.

For Canada, Sukhjinder Singh took three wickets, while Kaleem Sana and Shail Patel claimed two each.

The defeat leaves Nepal on 28 points from 35 matches, with one game remaining against Oman on Monday. Canada have completed their campaign with 29 points.

title: Nepal PM, president stress unity and social harmony in Dashain messages - The Times of India
description: Nepal PM, president stress unity and social harmony in Dashain messages  The Times of India
publisher.title: The Times of India
full_article:
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah and President Ramchandra Paudel share heartfelt festive wishes for Bada Dashain, underlining family cohesion and social harmony. (Pic Credit: IANS)

PM remembers victims of devastating floods

President Paudel stresses harmony and cultural identity



You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.



Nepal Prime minister Balendra Shah and president Ramchandra Paudel on Saturday conveyed their greetings to the people on Bada Dashain, also known as Vijaya Dashami , the country's biggest festival, highlighting its importance in fostering family ties, social harmony and national unity.Their messages were issued on Phulpati, the seventh day of the 15-day Dashain festival. The occasion signals the start of the main festive period, when government offices close and celebrations gather momentum across Nepal.In his message, Prime Minister Shah said his government was committed to generating employment opportunities and promoting prosperity within the country so that Nepalis would not be compelled to travel abroad in search of work, according to the news agency PTI.Describing Bada Dashain as a festival that brings families together, Shah said it strengthens relationships, encourages unity and fosters closer bonds among people. He noted that the festival's religious, cultural and social significance had also helped connect Nepalis living across different parts of the world.“The sky itself feels different, the earth carries a unique fragrance, and the surroundings become naturally filled with joy and exuberance,” he said, describing the festive atmosphere.Shah observed that Nepalis had continued to celebrate Dashain and preserve their religious, cultural and social traditions despite numerous challenges over the years.Referring to the recent devastating flash floods in Bhotekoshi, Shah said this year's festivities had arrived while the country was still mourning the loss of lives and damage caused by the disaster. The floods left 1,455 people dead, 5,285 missing and more than 13,000 rescued, according to the figures cited in his message.The prime minister offered prayers for those who lost their lives, wished the injured a speedy recovery and expressed condolences to the affected families. He added that the government was working urgently to rehabilitate people displaced by the disaster.Shah also highlighted the traditional exchange of tika and jamara during Dashain. Tika, a mixture of vermilion powder, curd and rice, and jamara, consisting of barley shoots, are received from elders as symbols of respect for senior family members and affection for younger relatives.Nepalis traditionally receive tika and jamara from elders on Dashami, the festival's tenth day, which falls on October 21 this year.In a separate message, president Ramchandra Paudel extended his wishes for happiness, peace, prosperity, good health and continued progress to Nepalis living both within the country and abroad.Paudel said that while Nepal's diverse ethnic and religious communities follow their own customs and traditions, Bada Dashain plays a significant role in bringing families together and promoting social harmony, forgiveness, goodwill and fraternity.He added that the festival helps strengthen unity across Nepal's geographical, cultural and linguistic diversity while safeguarding the country's cultural identity.
